opening: Over a smartphone, a daughter begs for a life to be spared and a kidnapper shouts: bring one hundred million yen alone by noon tomorrow, or this hostage dies; no police. Hearing the demand, her father decides the ransom should not be paid. Why?
reference_answer:
The father is the hostage. His wealthy daughter is free and receives the kidnapper’s phone call.
The father hears the kidnapper order his daughter to bring the ransom alone. He fears that, once she arrives with the money, the kidnapper will kill both of them to eliminate witnesses.
His daughter is his only family. To protect her, he tells her not to pay the ransom or come to the meeting, even though refusing puts his own life at risk.
The explanation concerns the father’s fear and decision; it does not establish that the kidnapper eventually kills either of them.

public_history.text: The father is himself the hostage. He is being held captive by the kidnapper, who has forced or allowed a phone call in which the daughter pleads for his life and the kidnapper demands that she bring one hundred million yen alone by noon the next day, with no police. Hearing this, the father realizes that the only way the ransom can be paid is for his daughter to come alone to the kidnapper—walking straight into danger herself. Rather than let that happen, he decides the ransom should not be paid. His refusal is a deliberate sacrifice: he would rather his own life remain at risk than have his daughter deliver the money and fall into the kidnapper's hands.

label_boundaries: The six USER_20261111_TS034_Qxxx examples preserve user-confirmed original Host labels for the exact quoted questions and their supplied histories. These specific precedents take priority for those exact cases; do not infer an established unconditional killing plan or eventual outcome from them.

An unqualified question about the father fearing danger to his daughter includes his feared future ransom meeting, not only present hostage status. Historical acceptance of a core reconstruction does not override current full-story completion requirements.

Distinguish the father’s fear from the kidnapper’s actual plan or a certain outcome: he fears the kidnapper might kill both if his daughter comes with the money, to remove witnesses. Do not say the kidnapper has decided to kill the father regardless of payment, will actually do so, or has disclosed such a plan.

When asked whether the father refuses because he knows he will be killed regardless of payment, answer no: that substitutes an unsupported cause for his established protective motive. If asked whether the kidnapper would kill the father regardless of payment, or has no intention of releasing him, without attributing this as the known motive, the material counterfactual is unspecified: answer yes and no. Do not treat earlier host labels or player guesses as evidence.

A question about whether the father fears he may be killed after the daughter arrives with the ransom can be affirmed as fear, not as a certain plan or outcome. A question that merely says the ransom is paid, without saying who arrives or whether the kidnapper would kill regardless, must not turn the conditional fear into certainty.

When a question combines the established fact that the father is captive with the unestablished claim that the captor has no intention of releasing him or plans to kill him regardless, return yes and no: captivity is established, while the captor’s unconditional plan is unknown. A question claiming this unsupported belief is the reason for refusal instead receives no.
